implementation_notes: Compose's tree-scoped key: a CompositionLocal is created with compositionLocalOf (reads are tracked, only readers recompose) or staticCompositionLocalOf (no read tracking, the whole content lambda recomposes when the value changes, which is cheaper for values that never change). CompositionLocalProvider(LocalX provides value) { content } publishes it for the Composition below, and descendants read LocalX.current - the pattern MaterialTheme is built from. The Android documentation explicitly discourages overuse because implicit dependencies are harder to reason about and to debug.
pitfalls: Providing a screen's ViewModel through a CompositionLocal is called out as bad practice: descendants end up depending on a whole object instead of the values they use, and previews/tests must provide it.
staticCompositionLocalOf does not track reads, so using it for a changing value recomposes the entire content lambda - choose it only for values that never change.
A CompositionLocal without a default forces every test and @Preview to provide it; giving it a plausible default instead can hide a provider that is missing in production.

variants.name: CoroutineContext element inherited down the coroutine tree
variants.idiom_name: custom CoroutineContext.Element + coroutineContext[Key], withContext to rebind
variants.implementation_notes: The coroutine context is a set of elements that child coroutines inherit from their parent scope, so a custom element (like CoroutineName) is readable at any depth with coroutineContext[Key] and never has to appear in a suspend signature; withContext(RequestId(id)) rebinds the element for a nested scope and restores the outer value afterwards. Use it server-side for request or trace context, where there is no UI tree to hang a CompositionLocal on; use CompositionLocal in Compose UI code.
pitfalls: Elements that share a Key cannot coexist: adding a second one with the same key silently replaces the first instead of merging.
coroutineContext[Key] returns null when the element was never provided - there is no compile-time guarantee that an ancestor bound it.
Everything below inherits the element, so a per-request value that outlives its request is readable by unrelated later work unless the scope is closed properly.
